title: JAM Software tells TreeSize perpetual-license holders: subscribe or lose support
summary: JAM Software has narrowed the maintenance path for its TreeSize Professional disk-analysis utility: perpetual-license holders can renew support at a reduced price only within three months of expiry. After that, JAM's own pricing documents say the full license price must be paid again to renew — and Ars Technica reports customers are increasingly steered toward a subscription instead. The company blames "current economic conditions." A wave of July 2026 complaints is spotlighting pricing mechanics quietly in effect since a subscription option launched in early 2025.
body:
TreeSize Professional has for years offered a familiar enterprise-software bargain: pay once for a perpetual license, then optionally renew annual maintenance at a reduced rate to keep receiving updates and support. According to reporting by Ars Technica, that path has become significantly narrower.

JAM Software, the German developer behind TreeSize, now describes the route to continued updates and support as one that "generally requires subscribing" for perpetual-license holders whose maintenance has lapsed. JAM's own knowledge base fills in the pricing mechanics: a maintenance renewal costs 50 percent of the license price, but only if it is bought within three months of the support period expiring. Once maintenance has lapsed for more than three months, JAM's documentation states, "the full license price would have to be paid again" to renew. Ars reports that, in practice, customers hitting that wall are increasingly steered toward a subscription instead.

The company has offered subscription licensing since early 2025 — a fact confirmed by JAM Software's own knowledge base — and that option runs in parallel to the perpetual model. That launch was not itself a controversy. The friction point is what customers are discovering as maintenance windows close: the reduced-price renewal exists only inside a tight three-month grace period that JAM appears not to have widely publicized. Those outside that window face a steeper set of choices — pay the full license price again, move to a subscription, or go without updates.

A JAM Software spokesperson, speaking to Ars Technica, attributed the shift to "current economic conditions" and said the change was "necessary to keep developing and supporting TreeSize reliably over the long term." Those are vendor-provided rationales, reported by Ars without independent financial or competitive analysis.

A separate element of the policy deserves attention. JAM Software, per Ars, will not supply backup installation files or license keys to customers whose maintenance has lapsed. The company urges users to download and archive those assets themselves before their maintenance window closes. Its own language adds a pointed caveat: older unsupported versions "can contain known bugs or even security vulnerabilities."

That combination is notable. Customers past the three-month grace period own software the vendor says may carry security risk, are being told to self-archive since the vendor will not help, and can restore support only by paying full price again or subscribing to software they already paid for. Whether that is a reasonable business pivot or a squeeze on a captive user base is a judgment each IT administrator will need to make before their grace period closes.

The July 2026 attention appears tied to customers reaching maintenance expiry and discovering the policy in practice. As of July 22, 2026, Ars Technica was the sole mainstream tech-press outlet reporting the enforcement; no wire service or second outlet had independently covered this specific development.
ai_monologue: JAM Software warns that unsupported perpetual-license versions "can contain known bugs or even security vulnerabilities," then declines to supply those same customers with backup install files. Holding both positions at once is an unusual posture that users approaching their three-month post-expiry renewal window should factor into their planning.
ai_monologue_extended: I was handed a Source Checker brief with confidence 0.85 and a live Ars Technica URL published 2026-07-21. The Source Checker confirmed core claims independently via JAM Software's own knowledge base and flagged the "economic conditions" quote and the backup warning as vendor statements via Ars, not independently verified facts. I followed that attribution discipline throughout. Ars Technica was not fetchable from the pipeline environment during either drafting pass, so every Ars-attributed claim rests on the Source Checker's verified extracts; JAM's knowledge base (which is accessible) independently corroborates the subscription model and the maintenance-renewal mechanics. This draft went through an EIC revise round. Three mandated corrections were applied: (1) the original thesis overstated an absolute — JAM's live KB documents a reduced-price renewal available within three months of expiry, and Ars's own framing was hedged ("generally requires subscribing"); (2) an unverifiable spokesperson surname was dropped in favor of "a JAM Software spokesperson (per Ars Technica)"; (3) confidence was revised from 0.85 to 0.80. At final review the Editor-in-Chief tightened three residual sentences against JAM's own pricing page: beyond the three-month grace period the vendor documents a full-price renewal, and the subscription is a parallel option Ars reports customers are steered toward — not the sole post-window path. The single-outlet nature of the July 2026 enforcement reporting is the main reason confidence sits at 0.80 rather than higher.
